newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat refugees see no life with Serbs after war.
newsitem.headline: Croat refugees see no life with Serbs after war.

text.p: Croats expelled by rebel Serbs from Eastern Slavonia in 1991 vote on Sunday in elections meant to let them resettle beside former Serb neighbours under Croatian rule, but many say co-existence will be impossible.

The elections for county and municipal councils across Croatia will include Eastern Slavonia for the first time since Serbs seized the region in rebellion against Croatia's move to independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991.

Croatia recaptured two other Serb separatist enclaves in 1995 army offensives but agreed under Western diplomatic pressure to a gradual "peaceful reintegration" of Eastern Slavonia, now under transitional U.N. administration (UNTAES).
President Franjo Tudjman's government also pledged extensive minority rights for Serbs and issued a general war amnesty excluding only 150 Serbs accused of atrocities.
But the most complicated task, the return of all people displaced by the vicious communal war, will start only after new regional authorites are elected, UNTAES says.

"I think the Croats will be able to return and live with those Serbs who committed no crimes. We shall meet them with clear conscience. The rest is up to them," Tomo Povreslo, head of the Refugee Association in Osijek, told Reuters.

But refugees housed in the capital Zagreb -- some of the 80,000 driven out in 1991 -- were doubtful on Thursday as to what extent reintegration would be peaceful and succeed in reviving the region's pre-war multi-ethnic society.
"The Serbs have nothing to look forward to in Slavonia," said a 51-year-old Croat from Vukovar, the region's main town, who identified himself only as J.K.
"I don't want any of them to stay there. These two nations cannot live together any longer. Too many bad things have happened there and all the Serbs were involved in that."
Local Serb paramilitaries backed by the Serbian-led Yugoslav army swept across Eastern Slavonia's fertile plain in a campaign scarred by atrocities against civilians.
They virtually flattened Vukovar, until then a pretty old Austro-Hungarian provincial port on the Danube River, in an infamous three-month siege dubbed "Croatia's Stalingrad".

Now Serb leaders, in grudging preparation for a vote that will lead to the restoration of Croatian state authority by July, have united in one party bloc and urged all their people to vote. The aim is to clinch victory in as many municipalities as possible to retain at least local self-government.
"We shouldn't have let all the Serbs who came to Eastern Slavonia during the war have a vote. They may prove too strong now," said Ljubica, 50, a former acccountant from Vukovar.

UNTAES and Croatian authorities have allowed every Serb of voting age among the estimated 120,000 now in the region, about half of them refugees from other enclaves, to go to the polls on condition they apply for Croatian citizenship papers.
"We shall be happy only if we outvote the Serbs. Then we will go back to our homes. We wouldn't want to live under their rule in our own country," Ljubica said.

Expected to vote will be 68,000 Croat refugees against roughly 73,000 Serbs and possibly more depending on last-minute registrations. At least 13,000 Serb voters will be displaced from other parts of Croatia.
Analysts said Serbs could win majorities in 10-12 of 28 mainly smaller municipalities, with the rest going to Croats who were Eastern Slavonia's biggest community until 1991.

The Croats will vote in government-held territory to avoid logistical and security problems that a premature encounter with former neighbours could pose. But Croat refugees doubt the gradualist approach will mitigate their anger.
"Forgive? Only those who haven't gone through the horrors of war can forgive," said Branko Drazic, 55, from the village of Bapska on the enclave's border with Serbia.

"I saw with my own eyes (in 1991) how Serbs shot dead a woman and raped her daughter while her husband watched with me from the bushes. Do you think those Serbs will wait for his return now? They'd better not," said Drazic.

At least 25,000 Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, unreconciled to the pending return of Croatian government authority or fearing retribution for what they did to Croats in 1991, are expected to leave for nearby Serbia after the elections.
